analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction corporations get for paying any employee over $1 million.
analysis.headline: Introduced with nine Senate sponsors and sent to the Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any action since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: Current tax law lets corporations deduct all employee pay as a business expense, except that they cannot deduct pay above $1 million for their five highest-paid executives — and even that cap is waived for pay structured as performance bonuses. This bill extends the $1 million deduction cap to every individual performing services for a publicly held corporation, keeps the cap on former CEOs, CFOs, and top-paid officers, closes a gap that let recently deregistered companies escape the rules, and directs the Treasury to write rules blocking companies from dodging the cap by routing pay through other entities. The result would be higher taxes on corporations and on people earning more than $1 million a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers as a whole, through higher revenue and a smaller deficit share, since the lost deductions would have been claimed by corporations and their highest-paid people. It also restores the principle that the tax code should not help corporations write off eight-figure pay packages.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the existing $1 million executive pay deduction cap from a company's five highest-paid executives to every individual performing services for the corporation, directly or indirectly.

Keeps the cap applied to former principal executive and financial officers and to officers who were among the three highest-paid in earlier years, preventing companies from avoiding the cap by rotating executives out.

Expands the definition of a publicly held corporation to include companies that were required to file reports with the SEC at any point in the previous three years, closing a gap where companies could escape the cap by dropping their SEC filing status.
Directs the Treasury Department to write rules to prevent avoidance of the cap, including pay routed through a pass-through or other entity.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that pay anyone more than $1 million a year, and those highly paid individuals themselves — largely executives at large public companies, top Wall Street traders, and other seven-figure earners at public firms. Companies would owe tax on pay above $1 million that they currently deduct.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations and people earning over $1 million

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the existing performance-based compensation exception in place, so companies can still deduct large payouts by structuring them as incentive pay, which limits how much revenue the bill actually raises.

Applying the cap to every individual performing services for the company — not just executives — would add compliance complexity and higher tax costs for firms with many million-dollar earners, such as large banks, and could put them at a disadvantage against private or foreign competitors.

Because the cap applies per individual rather than to pay practices generally, companies have an incentive to reorganize how compensation is delivered, some of which the Treasury would have to police through new regulations that take time and can be contested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on a narrow group — corporations and people already earning over $1 million a year — while the revenue benefits every federal taxpayer in some measure. The main honest concern is effectiveness: the preserved performance-pay exception and the breadth of the covered population mean the bill could be more complicated to administer than its headline suggests, and companies would likely restructure pay to blunt part of it. As a matter of who bears the burden, the design is straightforward: the people paying are the people the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on May 1, 2025, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors and one independent.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral is the last entry in its action history.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled or taken on the bill since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly held corporations and their highest-paid employees, who continue to deduct unlimited compensation because the bill has not moved. Nothing has been decided yet — the bill simply has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations and million-dollar earners, for now

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill expanding the executive pay deduction cap and issued introductory remarks.

for.name: Senate cosponsors (7 Democrats and 1 independent, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Whitehouse, and Blumenthal)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill its entire Senate support from one party's caucus.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote since its referral in May 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors are Democrats or the independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill sits with the Republican-chaired Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill eliminates their federal tax deduction for any compensation above $1 million per person, a subsidy they currently receive. Their interest in keeping the deduction runs directly against taxpayers who would otherwise fund it.

industries.industry: Highly compensated executives and employees at public companies
industries.note: Anyone at a public company earning more than $1 million a year would see the tax value of their excess pay eliminated. This group's gain under current law comes at ordinary taxpayers' expense.

industries.industry: Executive compensation consultants and corporate tax advisors
industries.note: Expanding and reworking the deduction cap would create new demand for advice on restructuring pay and complying with the rules, though strong anti-avoidance rules could also limit some of that work.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action more than a year into the session, the realistic path is that the bill dies in committee without a vote, as most tax bills without bipartisan sponsorship do. Its best chance would be being folded into a broader tax or budget package, which has not been indicated.
